query: Reported superconducting high-entropy alloys are dominated by Nb-Ta matrices, while other studies concern titanium-rich systems based on heavy transition metals and partly ordered systems. Consequently, these precedents do not establish what controls superconductivity in high-entropy alloys outside the best-studied material classes. Within the defining constraint of a solid solution containing at least five elements at no less than 5 atomic percent each, what governs superconducting behavior in such an uncharacterized high-entropy alloy, and why? State one testable mechanistic hypothesis, a controlled comparison against the starting material, predicted observations relative to the baseline, applicable boundary conditions, the earlier evidence supporting the hypothesis, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In a five-element refractory high-entropy alloy outside the canonical Nb–Ta and Ti-based systems, introducing at least 5 at% of an additional element (e.g., Sc) modifies local bonding and increases the electronic density of states near the Fermi level, thereby raising the superconducting critical temperature (Tc) relative to an undoped baseline.
generation.material_initial_state: An arc-melted, equimolar five-element refractory high-entropy alloy (HEA) forming a single-phase solid solution with a baseline Tc in the range of 5–8 K.
generation.intervention: Add ≥5 at% of scandium (Sc) to the baseline HEA composition via arc melting and rapid solidification, ensuring a retained single-phase solid solution.
generation.conditions: Structural and superconductivity measurements down to cryogenic temperatures (2–10 K) under identical thermal history to compare undoped (baseline) versus Sc-doped samples.
generation.structural_mediator: Local compositional variations and short-range order that alter electron-phonon coupling and the density of states near the Fermi level.
generation.mechanism: Addition of Sc reduces partial ordering and increases the effective valence electron concentration, promoting stronger BCS-type electron-phonon interactions and thus higher Tc.
generation.predicted_outcome: Sc-doped samples will exhibit an increase of approximately 0.5–1 K in superconducting transition temperature and enhanced superconducting volume fraction compared to the undoped baseline.
generation.baseline: An unmodified five-element refractory HEA with stable single-phase structure and a known Tc around 5–8 K.
generation.boundary: If doping causes secondary phases or phase segregation, the effect on Tc may be suppressed or non-monotonic. The result holds as long as the composition remains a single-phase solid solution.
generation.uncertainty: The precise size of the Tc increase depends on the resulting local chemical order and phase stability, which remain unverified for new compositions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of samples with 0, 5, and 10 at% Sc substitution. Confirm single-phase structure by X-ray diffraction, then measure Tc via four-point resistivity and magnetic susceptibility down to 2 K.
measurements: X-ray diffraction for phase identification and lattice parameters
Resistivity as a function of temperature
Magnetic susceptibility to determine superconducting transition
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Sc-containing samples do not show any shift of the superconducting transition temperature (Tc) or if Tc decreases despite maintaining a single-phase structure, the hypothesis would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: To overcome these shortfalls, refractory elements are frequently alloyed with other refractory elements, occasionally with an addition of a non-refractory element (such as Al). When five or more elements are alloyed in near-equimolar concentrations, crystalline random solid solutions or partially ordered ones may sometimes form, termed high-entropy alloys (HEAs) [,]. A well-studied refractory HEA system is Hf-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr, which demonstrates decent RT ductility and solid solution strengthening at high temperatures [,,,,,,]. This HEA is historically also the first superconducting HEA []. In a search for the enhancement of physical-mechanical properties of the Hf-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr refractory HEAs, we have employed the additional alloying element, scandium (Sc). Formally classified as a rare-earth element, scandium possesses a relatively high melting temperature Tm= 1541 °C and has a low density of 2.985 gcm−3. Alloying small amounts of Sc (a few %) into aluminum alloys has been demonstrated to cause a beneficial strengthening effect due to the formation of Al3Sc intermetallic precipitates [], making the Sc-Al lightweight alloys for aerospace components the main application of scandium. The superconductivity of disordered materials has been extensively studied because of an observation made on the insulator-superconductor transition or disorder-induced superconductivity. In addition, recent studies on BiS2-based layered superconductors have shown the importance of controlling the local structural disorder to improve superconducting properties. As a new category of disordered superconductors, high-entropy alloys (HEAs), which are alloys containing five or more elements with an atomic concentration between 5 and 35%,, have been extensively studied, leading to the discovery of a wide range of HEA superconductors. One of the notable features is the difference in characteristics of superconductivity among conventional metal or alloy superconductors, superconducting thin films, and HEA superconductors,. Namely, the dependence of Tc on valence electron count (VEC) for HEAs exhibits interesting trends when that was compared with those for classical alloys (metals) and amorphous alloys.
